scenes.text: Fair warning. [pause] This is an embellished fictional dramatization that <emphasis>may or may not</emphasis> be based on true stories. The narrator is a guy named Charlie Hack, and any resemblance to me is mostly coincidental. Names, characters, companies and events are fictitious, or used fictitiously.
This preview drops you into the <emphasis>middle</emphasis> of the book. Part Three. [pause] It's called C Things That Looked Like A Things.
scenes.tts: This preview drops you into the <emphasis>middle</emphasis> of the book. Part Three. [pause] It's called C Things That Looked Like Ay Things.

scenes.text: Silicon Valley is very good at telling a story about A players. The people who look like they were always going to win, and the companies that look like they were always going to work.
scenes.tts: Silicon Valley is very good at telling a story about Ay players. The people who look like they were always going to win, and the companies that look like they were always going to work.

scenes.text: The myth is a straight line: a garage, a genius, a ticker symbol. But most of the real work looks nothing like that. It looks like another ordinary Tuesday, doing the next right thing.

And from the outside, a C thing can look like an A thing. [pause] The applause is loud, and the real work is quieter. This book is about that gap, between what people saw and what was really going on.
scenes.tts: And from the outside, a C thing can look like an Ay thing. [pause] The applause is loud, and the real work is quieter. This book is about that gap, between what people saw and what was really going on.

scenes.text: A C player is not a failure. It's the person who was never the smartest in the room, and kept going anyway. [pause] Because there is always the smarter guy in the room. The richer guy, the more experienced, the wisest. Stay humble. Stay curious.

The Valley falls in love with products. Specific wins, in specific years. I got more out of building a <emphasis>platform</emphasis>: a foundation you can stand on, then build the next thing on, and the thing after that.
You don't invent a career in one move. You stack building blocks: habits, fundamentals, the unglamorous layer nobody puts on a slide. [pause] That layer is what you actually stand on later.
<slow>It's all relative, how good you look from the outside.</slow> [pause] But one thing stayed for certain. <emphasis>I just kept going.</emphasis> And I kept doing my best.
Then the work itself changed. [pause] I'm usually the most excited person in the room about A.I. Which is funny, because I should be the <emphasis>saddest</emphasis>.

Because A.I. came after the code writers first. [pause] In my own work, A.I. now writes essentially all of the code I ship. That's how I work. Not a measured team result. Not a general industry figure.

So software engineering practices have to be geared around that. That's what Software Engineering 101 and 201 are about, and it's the second half of this book: how to work now, and how companies should use A.I.

The book begins with a green-screen dream, and it ends by dreaming about A.I. This part, in the middle, is the turn. [pause] It's free. It's open. And when version one is ready, if you were around for any of it, you get to tell your side. [pause] The story is still being written.
Silicon Valley C Players. Coming in 2027.
